title: Sizing slipstream: transient workspace, alloc-retry modes, and fragmentation hypotheses
content:
Goal / context:
Quick notes on a different angle of memory fragmentation and OOMs: how transient per-request workspace sizing interacts with cudaMalloc retry modes and host-side heuristics to produce ‘slipstream’ OOM patterns (short, high-frequency OOM spikes not explained by long-term leak/retention). This doc collects observations, microbenchmarks, and short proposals.

Key observation summary (TL;DR):
- We see short (<2s) OOM spikes correlated with bursts of requests that have slightly larger peak working set than the long-term steady state.
- Under heavy pressure, cudaMalloc sometimes returns ENOMEM quickly, then a retry path (our runtime's async retry) succeeds after ~100–400ms — during which request processing stalls and the system falls back to smaller model variants for some routes.
- The allocator’s small-slab fragmentation + large ephemeral allocations (activation buffers, temporary attention scratchpads) create patterns where available contiguous blocks exist but are split across many tombstoned regions; a single large cudaMalloc fails even though total free >= requested.
- The incidents are not classic persistent leaks: RSS on the node does not steadily increase and fragmentation heatmaps show spikes then gradual reclamation.

Reproducer notes (quick synthetic):
- Simple harness: sequentially start N threads each doing: allocate transient tensors pattern A (mix of 30–600MiB), free, then allocate pattern B (single large allocation ~1GiB) with random jitter. Repeat 5000x.
- With pool disabled (cudamallocasync off) we see frequent immediate ENOMEM. With pool on + small-slab arenas tuned low, behaviour is: more short ENOMEMs but more successful retries on second attempt.
- Commands used: 
  - nvidia-smi dmon, pmon for baseline
  - NVPROF-level traces for a failing alloc scope (capture cudaMalloc calls and elapsed)
  - envs toggled: RUNTIME_ALLOC_MODE=async_retry|failfast, CUDAMALLOCASYNC_MAX_ARENAS=8|32, POOL_CHUNK=16MiB|64MiB

Telemetry excerpts (what to collect going forward):
- allocation request histogram by size (buckets 4KiB, 32KiB, 512KiB, 8MiB, 64MiB, 256MiB, 1GiB)
- failure + retry traces: timestamped pair (malloc-size, free-space-total, contiguous-largest, free-block-count)
- per-request peak working set (including KV-cache reservations) and sequence length
- timeline of allocator arena counts + decommit events

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Contiguous-block starvation: many freed small blocks produce many holes; a large allocation fails because they are fragmented. Contiguous-largest metric will drop sharply before an OOM spike.
2) Arena overprovision & stale shadow slab: allocator keeps many small arenas that are largely free but not coalesced — coalescing is expensive so it’s deferred; during short bursts coalescing cannot keep up.
3) Host-side paging/migrate delays: unified-memory/prefetch steps (on some instances we saw cudaMemPrefetchAsync activity) delay availability for large contiguous region requests.
4) Retry bias mask: our async retry window currently uses exponential backoff up to 500ms. That window sometimes bridges the transient fragmentation gap but causes head-of-line stalling.

Evidence collected so far:
- Heatmaps: fragmentation-locality heatmaps show many small freed blocks around the same stream id. When B pattern tries to allocate a 1GiB buffer, allocator does a first-fit scan, fails, then small-window retries succeed after other streams finish and free or coalesce.
- CC: observed >50% of short OOMs occurred when KV-cache eviction and per-request workspace allocations were concurrent; suggests contention between long-lived caches and transient buffers.
- With smaller arena chunk sizes (16MiB) we saw higher free-block-count but lower contiguous-largest leading to more immediate failures for big allocations.

Quick experiments to run (prioritized):
- A: Measure contiguous-largest over time under controlled workload that ramps transient-peak to identify threshold where 1GiB malloc fails.
- B: Toggle coalescing aggressiveness: instrument allocator to do opportunistic coalesce on free if fragmentation score > X (cheap linear scan). Compare latency/OOM tradeoffs.
- C: Try transient-prefetch suppression: for requests that will soon request a large contiguous allocation, we can throttle KV-cache reclamation to avoid creating many small holes at once. (Counterintuitive but might reduce simultaneous churn.)
- D: Patch RUNTIME_ALLOC_MODE=failfast for specific routes where we prefer fallback (smaller model) instead of head-of-line blocking on retry. Measure user-visible latency/regressions.

Mitigation proposals (short-term):
- Soft-reserve: reserve a small contiguous region per worker (configurable, e.g., 512MiB) that is only used for large allocations; this avoids fragmentation-induced failures at the cost of static reservation.
- Opportunistic compaction task: background thread that scans and coalesces adjacent free blocks during low-util windows; should be cancellable when node becomes busy.
- Per-request hinting API (low-effort): request can declare its peak contiguous demand ("peak_hint_bytes"). Runtime can preferentially satisfy hints by allocating from reserved pools or preemptively defragmenting.
- Retry policy tuning: reduce retries for routes that have fallbacks; increase for critical routes that must attempt to serve (but cap at 200ms).

Longer-term ideas (research):
- Compaction primitives in CUDA: investigate if we can leverage cudaMemAdvise + migrate to reduce fragmentation footprint across GPUs.
- Slab-aware KV-cache layout: split long-lived KV-cache into chunk sizes matching allocator chunk grain to reduce binary fragmentation footprints.
- Kernel-level coalescer: collaboration with allocator team to expose cheap coalescing hints so the runtime can mark certain free sequences for immediate coalescing.

Open questions / unknowns (to triage):
- Why do some machines show more slipstream OOMs than others with same workload? Possible differences in GPU driver versions, numa layout, or CUDA allocation algorithm. Need to matrix driver/CUDA versions.
- Are we seeing interaction with cudaMallocAsync heuristic decommit timing? (I suspect arenas decommit too aggressively or in a way that fragments.)
- How does our background tracer affect coalescing? (tracing could delay free callbacks)

Actionable next steps (this sprint):
- [Owner: Aisha] Run contiguous-largest telemetry sweep on canary fleet (SRV-1248). Collect 24h baseline and during synthetic ramp.
- [Owner: Liam] Implement cheap coalesce-on-free flag behind a runtime toggle; measure extra CPU overhead and fragmentation index (perf-331).
- [Owner: Gabriela] Benchmark soft-reserve tradeoffs (0, 256MiB, 512MiB, 1GiB) on dedicated pool nodes. Add cost model numbers (delta in effective capacity per node).
- Add ticket to product: define policy for failfast routes vs retry-prefer routes.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Avoid global defrag at hot time; prefer per-worker small compaction windows and per-route hints.
- Consider adding contiguous-largest metric to console (useful for oncall to triage).
- Some short OOMs may be mitigated by ordering allocations differently inside kernels (alloc larger ones first). Worth a quick patch in the op scheduler.

References / links:
- allocator microbench harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/main/tools/malloc-harness (local branch: alloc-slipstream)
- initial thread: Slack #serving-runtime t03G4k2 (alloc-retry discussion)

Appendix: quick sample log snippet (real-looking)
[2024-11-03T16:12:04.123Z] worker-12 stream-7 alloc(1073741824) -> ENOMEM (contiguous-largest=512MiB, free-total=1.2GiB, free-block-count=124)
[2024-11-03T16:12:04.224Z] worker-12 stream-7 retry(1) sleep 120ms
[2024-11-03T16:12:04.345Z] worker-12 stream-7 alloc(1073741824) -> OK (from arena-3)

Unresolved: is it better to do soft-reserve or smarter KV-cache placement? both probably needed.

-- Aisha
